cloze.text: The {{c1::Physician's Desk Reference (PDR)}} can provide information on drugs, side effects, names, etc.
A drug's {{c1::brand (trade)}} name is the manufacturer's name, written with the first letter {{c2::capitalized}} (e.g., Valium®, Tylenol®).
A drug's {{c1::generic}} name names its chemical makeup and is written in {{c2::lowercase}} (e.g., diazepam, acetaminophen).
cloze.extra: Generic drugs (marketed without brand names) are less expensive than brand-name drugs.

cloze.text: The generic name of Valium® (Vazepam®) is {{c1::diazepam}}; the generic name of Tylenol® is {{c2::acetaminophen}}.
Generic drugs marketed without brand names are {{c1::less expensive}} than brand-name drugs.
{{c1::Synergism}}: getting more than the desired effects when taking two drugs together ({{c2::1 + 1 > 2}}).
Example of synergism: {{c1::oxycodone}} + {{c2::acetaminophen}} = Percocet®.
Enteral administration uses the {{c1::GI tract}}; it is the {{c2::safest, slowest, and most variable}} route.
Oral route: the drug is swallowed (e.g., {{c1::ibuprofen}}); it may cause GI upset because the drug is largely absorbed in the {{c2::small intestines}}.
Sublingual route: the drug is placed {{c1::under the tongue}} (e.g., Nitroglycerin®); {{c2::capillaries}} under the tongue speed up absorption.
The sublingual route is commonly used for {{c1::nitrates}} (for cardiac conditions).
The {{c1::sublingual}} and {{c2::rectal}} enteral routes avoid the first-pass effect.
{{c1::Parenteral}} administration: drug administered elsewhere in the body than the mouth and alimentary canal — it {{c2::bypasses the GI tract}}.
{{c1::Intravenous}} administration: drug directly enters the systemic circulation, giving {{c2::100%}} instant and complete availability in the bloodstream.
Intravenous administration is the best option to {{c1::control the level}} of drugs and is used in {{c2::emergency situations}} and {{c3::chemotherapy}}.
{{c1::Intramuscular}} injection uses muscles because of their high volume of {{c2::blood flow}} (e.g., EpiPen®).
Intramuscular absorption is rapid and is {{c1::increased}} when {{c2::massaging}} the area.
{{c1::Subcutaneous}} injection: drug injected under the skin but not into the muscles — useful for protein products such as {{c2::insulin}} that would otherwise be digested in the intestines.
{{c1::Intradermal}} injection: drug injected into the dermal layer (e.g., {{c2::allergy testing, TB skin test}}).
{{c1::Topical/transdermal}} route: drug applied to the body surface and absorbed slowly by capillaries under the skin (e.g., hydrocortisone, {{c2::nicotine patches}}).
With topical/transdermal drugs, more concentrated {{c1::toxicity}} should be carefully monitored.
Topical drug effects last a long time through slow absorption, but are less effective on {{c1::keratinized}} tissue.
Topicals include {{c1::ophthalmic}} (eye) and {{c2::otic}} (ear) preparations.
On a dose–response graph, the x-axis is {{c1::dose}} and the y-axis is {{c2::response}}.
{{c1::Therapeutic range}}: the range between the dose causing the minimum effect and the dose causing the minimum adverse effect.
{{c1::Therapeutic index (TI)}}: a number that determines the {{c2::safety}} of a drug.
Therapeutic index = {{c1::lethal dose (LD50)}} ÷ {{c2::effective dose (ED50)}}.
The {{c1::bigger}} the therapeutic index number, the safer the drug.
{{c1::Potency}}: the amount of drug needed to achieve the desired effect — the {{c2::less}} amount needed, the more potent the drug.
On a dose–response graph, the drug curve closest to the {{c1::left}} side is the most potent.
{{c1::Efficacy}}: the maximal response obtained by a drug ({{c2::Emax}}).
On a dose–response graph, the drug with the {{c1::highest point}} has the greatest efficacy.
Taking more of a drug will not increase its {{c1::efficacy}}, but will cause more {{c2::adverse reactions}}.
There is {{c1::no}} relationship between potency and efficacy.
cloze.extra: Book graph: Drug A (5 mg) and Drug B (50 mg) give the same 50% response, so A is more potent — but even though Drug B is less potent, at 500 mg it is 50% more efficacious.

cloze.text: All adverse reactions are {{c1::undesirable}} effects.
A {{c1::side effect}} acts on {{c2::non-target}} organs (e.g., xerostomia from antihypertensive meds).
A {{c1::toxic reaction}} is an {{c2::exaggerated effect on the target organ}} (e.g., barbiturate overdose → respiratory depression, death).
An {{c1::allergic reaction}} is an {{c2::immune hypersensitivity}} to a drug (e.g., swelling from benzocaine — Type I or IV).
Side effects and toxic reactions are {{c1::dose-related}} and {{c2::predictable}}; allergic reactions are neither.
The target of an allergic reaction is the {{c1::immune system}}.
Allergic reaction timing: Type I is {{c1::immediate (minutes–hours)}}; Type IV is {{c2::delayed (hours–days)}}.
Toxic reaction timing: {{c1::immediate to delayed}}, depending on the overdose level; side-effect timing depends on the drug.
Reversibility: side effects are {{c1::often reversible}}; toxic reactions depend on severity ({{c2::can be fatal}}); allergic reactions vary — {{c3::remove the allergen and treat}}.
Rate and efficiency of absorption depend on the {{c1::route of administration}}, the {{c2::pKa}} of the drug, drug {{c3::solubility}}, and the {{c4::pH}} of the media.
{{c1::Metabolism (biotransformation)}}: the process where the body breaks down/converts medication into other substances.
The {{c1::liver}} is the primary site for drug metabolism; other sites include {{c2::blood, lungs}}, etc.
{{c1::Seniors}}, {{c2::newborns}}, and patients with {{c3::liver malfunction}} may have difficulties metabolizing drugs.
{{c1::Elimination (excretion)}}: drugs and their metabolites are eliminated from the body.
Drug excretion occurs primarily in the {{c1::kidneys}}; drugs and metabolites are flushed out through {{c2::urine}}.
Each nephron contains a {{c1::glomerulus}}, a network of capillaries that performs the first step in filtering; it is surrounded by the thin-walled, bowl-shaped {{c2::Bowman's capsule}}.
Other sites of drug excretion: intestines, {{c1::saliva}}, {{c2::gingival crevicular fluid}}, sweat, tears, {{c3::breast milk}}, and lungs.
Renal excretion = {{c1::filtration}} − {{c2::reabsorption}} + {{c3::secretion}}.
The autonomic nervous system is part of the {{c1::peripheral}} nervous system and controls {{c2::involuntary}} actions such as the beating of the heart.
The autonomic nervous system includes the {{c1::sympathetic}} + {{c2::parasympathetic}} nervous systems.
The ANS is a major focus in pharmacology because many drugs either {{c1::stimulate or block}} it; it controls involuntary functions like heart rate, digestion, and salivation.
{{c1::Adrenergic}} = sympathetic nervous system (SANS); {{c2::cholinergic}} = parasympathetic nervous system (PANS).
Main neurotransmitters: sympathetic (adrenergic) — {{c1::epinephrine, norepinephrine}}; parasympathetic (cholinergic) — {{c2::acetylcholine}}.
cloze.extra: Acetylcholine mediates responses at the cholinergic receptors.

cloze.text: Adrenergic receptor subtypes: {{c1::α1}} — blood vessels; {{c2::β1}} — heart; {{c3::β2}} — lungs, skeletal muscle vessels, uterus.
Cholinergic {{c1::muscarinic}} receptors are found in the {{c2::salivary glands, heart, GI tract, bladder}}.
α1 activation → {{c1::vasoconstriction}}, ↑ BP.
β1 activation → ↑ {{c1::heart rate}}, ↑ {{c2::contractility}}.
β2 activation → {{c1::bronchodilation}}, vasodilation.
Cholinergic activation → ↑ saliva, ↑ GI motility, {{c1::↓}} heart rate, ↑ bladder contraction.
Adrenergic agonist {{c1::albuterol}} stimulates {{c2::β2}} receptors in the lungs → bronchodilator that treats asthma.
Adrenergic agonist {{c1::epinephrine}} prolongs local anesthesia and treats {{c2::anaphylaxis}}.
Cholinergic agonist {{c1::pilocarpine}} increases salivation — treats {{c2::xerostomia}}.
Adrenergic antagonists: {{c1::propranolol}} is a non-selective β-blocker; {{c2::atenolol}} is a selective β1-blocker.
Cholinergic antagonist {{c1::atropine}} {{c2::reduces}} saliva and {{c3::increases}} heart rate.
cloze.extra: Dental use: atropine may be used to reduce salivation before procedures.

cloze.text: Common side effects of adrenergic drugs: {{c1::tachycardia}}, anxiety, {{c2::tremors}}, {{c3::dry mouth}}.
cloze.extra: p.30 also lists cardiac arrhythmia and increased headaches/anxiety as adverse effects of adrenergic drugs.

cloze.text: Cholinergic AGONIST side effects: {{c1::excess saliva}}, diarrhea, {{c2::bradycardia}}.
Cholinergic ANTAGONIST side effects: {{c1::dry mouth}}, {{c2::blurred vision}}, {{c3::constipation}}.
Adrenergic drugs are contraindicated in {{c1::angina}}, {{c2::uncontrolled hypertension}}, and {{c3::(uncontrolled) hyperthyroidism}}.
Cholinergic drugs are contraindicated in {{c1::asthma}}, {{c2::cardiac disease}}, and {{c3::peptic ulcers}}.
cloze.extra: p.30: contraindicated for cardiac conditions because of side effects like a slowed heart rate.

cloze.text: Dental relevance: limit epinephrine to {{c1::0.04 mg}} (2 cartridges) in patients on {{c2::non-selective β-blockers}}.
cloze.extra: Adrenergics may also cause dry mouth.

cloze.text: The sympathetic nervous system (SANS) is the {{c1::fight or flight}} system.
Sympathetic adrenergic receptors: {{c1::alpha (α)}}, {{c2::beta-1 (β1)}}, {{c3::beta-2 (β2)}}.
{{c1::Adrenergic}} drugs stimulate adrenergic receptors and mimic the effects of the SANS.
{{c1::Antiadrenergic}} drugs block adrenergic receptors, produce the opposite effect of the SANS, and {{c2::decrease}} blood pressure.
Beta-blockers (suffix {{c1::-olol}}) {{c2::slow the heart rate}} and lower blood pressure.
The parasympathetic nervous system (PANS) creates {{c1::"rest and digest"}} responses.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: PARAsympathetic → PARAlyzed (from too much eating) → need to rest and digest.

cloze.text: PANS effects: pupils {{c1::return to normal}}; {{c2::slows}} heart rate and respiration; {{c3::decreases}} perspiration and arterial blood pressure.
PANS effects: {{c1::dilates}} blood vessels leading to the GI tract (↑ blood flow for digestion), {{c2::accelerates peristalsis}}, and stimulates salivary gland secretion.
{{c1::Cholinergic}} drugs stimulate cholinergic receptors and produce the effects of the PANS (e.g., pilocarpine).
{{c1::Anticholinergic}} drugs block cholinergic receptors and produce the opposite of rest and digest (e.g., atropine decreases salivation).
{{c1::Antihypertensive}} agents prevent and control high blood pressure.
{{c1::Beta blockers}} are NOT first-line for hypertension (used for comorbidities); diuretics, calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors and ARBs are first-line.
Diuretics block {{c1::sodium reabsorption}} in the {{c2::loop of Henle/distal tubule}} → ↓ blood volume and resistance.
Beta blockers block {{c1::β1}} (heart) ± {{c2::β2}} (lungs) → ↓ heart rate and contractility.
Calcium channel blockers inhibit {{c1::calcium influx}} in vascular smooth muscle → {{c2::vasodilation}}.
ACE inhibitors inhibit the ACE enzyme → block formation of {{c1::angiotensin II}}.
ARBs block {{c1::angiotensin II receptors}} → vasodilation.
Suffixes: diuretics {{c1::-ide}}; beta blockers {{c2::-olol}}; calcium channel blockers {{c3::-pine}} (mostly); ACE inhibitors {{c4::-pril}}; ARBs {{c5::-tan}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Diuretic → "DI" flipped → ID → -ide. Beta blocker → bb → flipped dd → olol. Calcium channel blocker → CC → with your credit card you bought a pint of beer (-pine). ARB → Arab countries have tan colored sand dunes (-tan).

cloze.text: Target sites: diuretics — {{c1::kidneys (nephron)}}; calcium channel blockers — {{c2::vascular smooth muscle and heart}}; ACE inhibitors and ARBs — the {{c3::renin-angiotensin system}}.
Primary effect: diuretics — ↓ {{c1::blood volume and preload}}; beta blockers — ↓ {{c2::heart rate and cardiac output}}; CCBs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs — {{c3::vasodilation}}.
Common side effects of diuretics: frequent urination, dehydration, {{c1::hypokalemia}}, dizziness.
Common side effects of beta blockers: fatigue, {{c1::bradycardia}}, {{c2::bronchoconstriction}} (non-selective), {{c3::masks hypoglycemia}}.
Common side effects of calcium channel blockers: {{c1::gingival hyperplasia}}, headache, flushing, hypotension.
Common side effects of ACE inhibitors: {{c1::dry cough}} (bradykinin-related), {{c2::angioedema}}, hypotension.
Common side effects of ARBs: dizziness, angioedema (rare), and {{c1::no dry cough}}.
Contraindications: diuretics — severe {{c1::renal impairment}}, dehydration; beta blockers — {{c2::asthma}} (non-selective), bradycardia.
Contraindications: calcium channel blockers — severe hypotension, {{c1::AV block}}; ACE inhibitors and ARBs — history of {{c2::angioedema}}, {{c3::pregnancy}}.
Dental relevance of diuretics: risk of {{c1::orthostatic hypotension}}, {{c2::dry mouth}}.
Dental relevance of calcium channel blockers: {{c1::gingival enlargement}}, especially with {{c2::nifedipine}}.
Other clinical uses: diuretics — {{c1::edema}}, CHF; beta blockers — angina, post-MI, arrhythmias, {{c2::anxiety}}.
Other clinical uses: calcium channel blockers — arrhythmias, {{c1::Raynaud's syndrome}}; ACE inhibitors and ARBs — heart failure, {{c2::diabetic nephropathy}}.

{{c1::Selective}} beta blockers block only β1 receptors in the heart — they slow the heart rate and lower BP without affecting breathing, so they are safer for patients with {{c2::asthma or lung conditions}}.
{{c1::Non-selective}} beta blockers block both β1 (heart) and β2 (lungs) — they lower BP but can cause {{c2::bronchoconstriction}}, dangerous for asthma or COPD.

basic.front: What is the first-pass effect, and why does it matter?
basic.back: The drug is metabolized in the GI tract and liver before it reaches the systemic circulation — this significantly reduces the amount of drug available.

basic.front: Why must epinephrine be limited to 0.04 mg (2 cartridges) in patients taking non-selective beta blockers?
basic.back: Their blood vessels can't dilate properly, increasing the risk of a dangerous spike in blood pressure.

mcq.question: A medication must reach 100% bioavailability immediately during a medical emergency. Which route is best?
mcq.explanation: IV puts the drug directly into the systemic circulation — 100% instant, complete availability, best control of drug level; used in emergencies. IM is rapid but still depends on absorption from muscle.

mcq.question: Nitroglycerin for angina is given sublingually mainly because this route:
options: A. Avoids the first-pass effect and absorbs quickly through capillaries under the tongue
B. Is the safest and slowest route
D. Allows absorption in the small intestine
mcq.answer: A. Avoids the first-pass effect and absorbs quickly through capillaries under the tongue
mcq.explanation: Sublingual capillaries speed absorption and the drug bypasses first-pass metabolism in the GI tract/liver. 100% instant availability describes IV only.

mcq.question: Drug X reaches a 50% response at 5 mg and plateaus at 50% efficacy. Drug Y reaches 50% at 50 mg and plateaus at 100%. Which statement is correct?
options: A. X is more potent; Y is more efficacious
B. X is more potent and more efficacious
C. Y is more potent; X is more efficacious
D. Both have the same potency
mcq.answer: A. X is more potent; Y is more efficacious
mcq.explanation: Potency = less drug needed for the effect (curve further left) → X. Efficacy = maximal response (highest point) → Y. Potency and efficacy are unrelated.

mcq.question: Which type of adverse drug reaction is neither dose-related nor predictable?
mcq.explanation: Allergic reactions are immune hypersensitivity — not dose-related, not predictable. Side effects and toxic reactions are both dose-related and predictable.

mcq.question: A patient taking propranolol needs local anesthesia. What is the appropriate precaution?
options: A. Limit epinephrine to 0.04 mg (2 cartridges)
mcq.answer: A. Limit epinephrine to 0.04 mg (2 cartridges)
mcq.explanation: Propranolol is a non-selective β-blocker. Epinephrine is limited to 0.04 mg because blocked β2 vessels can't dilate, so unopposed α1 vasoconstriction risks a dangerous BP spike. Local anesthesia itself is not contraindicated.

mcq.question: Which drug would be used to increase salivation in a patient with xerostomia?
mcq.explanation: Pilocarpine is a cholinergic agonist (stimulates muscarinic receptors → ↑ saliva). Atropine is the cholinergic antagonist that reduces saliva.

mcq.question: A patient's medication list includes amlodipine. Which oral finding is most likely related to this drug?
mcq.explanation: Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker (-pine); CCBs cause gingival hyperplasia/enlargement (especially nifedipine). A dry cough points to an ACE inhibitor.

mcq.question: A hypertensive patient reports a dry, persistent cough since starting a new medication. Which drug is most likely responsible?
mcq.explanation: Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor (-pril); dry cough (bradykinin-related) is its classic side effect. Losartan, an ARB, causes no dry cough.
